claims.claim: The acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) divides a recent (acute) load by a longer-term (chronic) load, typically a 1-week acute window over a 4-week chronic average. It is intended to indicate whether current load is appropriate relative to recent training and can be computed from session-RPE load, distance, or other load metrics; rolling sums or averages are used.
claims.evidence: Gabbett's model uses acute load (e.g., 1 week) and chronic load (e.g., 4-week average) and their ratio; Impellizzeri et al. describe the ACWR as acute weekly load divided by chronic load and note that different time windows and rolling or EWMA methods are used, which can produce different values.

citation.title: The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?

claims.claim: Gabbett's 'training-injury prevention paradox' proposes that high but appropriately progressed training loads build physical qualities that protect against injury, whereas rapid increases in load are a major cause of non-contact soft-tissue injury. The model claims the ACWR is a better predictor of injury than acute or chronic load alone.
claims.evidence: Gabbett 2016: 'Excessive and rapid increases in training loads are likely responsible for a large proportion of non-contact, soft-tissue injuries. However, physically hard (and appropriate) training develops physical qualities, which in turn protects against injuries.' The paper also states that 'the ratio of acute to chronic training load is a better predictor of injury than acute or chronic loads in isolation.'

citation.title: The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?

claims.topic: ACWR: proposed 'sweet spot' and its critique
claims.claim: The ACWR literature proposes a 'sweet spot' of approximately 0.8-1.3, with higher injury risk proposed above ~1.3-1.5 and below ~0.8. This is a heuristic model, not a validated precision threshold, and it has been criticized for lacking a physiological rationale and for methodological flaws.
claims.evidence: Impellizzeri et al. 2020 describe the proposed 'sweet spot' (0.8-1.3) and conclude that 'the physiological rationale for choosing this ratio is unknown' and that the ratio is 'well known to be problematic'; they also note that discretization and reference-category choices can inflate false discoveries. The sweet spot is commonly attributed to Blanch & Gabbett (2016).

citation.title: Training Load and Its Role in Injury Prevention, Part 2: Conceptual and Methodologic Pitfalls
citation.authors: Impellizzeri FM, McCall A, Ward P, Bornn L, Coutts AJ

claims.claim: ACWR has major methodological problems: the ratio does not properly normalize the numerator for the denominator (mathematical coupling), time windows and acute-load calculation methods are arbitrary, and discretization/reference-category choices inflate false discoveries. A 1,000-season simulation showed that an ACWR-injury association can be generated by training-schedule confounding even when no causal relationship exists.
claims.evidence: Impellizzeri et al. 2020: 'Lolli et al observed that the ACWR failed to normalize the numerator for the denominator'; 'Bornn et al created a 1000-season simulation ... the ACWR outside of the proposed "sweet spot" ... had a significant relationship with injury ... despite the simulation's being designed to have no relationship at all. Once the training day was considered ... the relationship ... no longer existed.'

citation.title: Training Load and Its Role in Injury Prevention, Part 2: Conceptual and Methodologic Pitfalls
citation.authors: Impellizzeri FM, McCall A, Ward P, Bornn L, Coutts AJ

claims.claim: A 2026 multilevel meta-analysis of 41 studies found that elevated ACWR had a small-to-moderate association with injury, with high heterogeneity; the association was not significant for time-loss injuries. The authors concluded that current evidence does not support ACWR as a stand-alone causal or predictive model.
claims.evidence: Ding et al. 2026: 'Elevated ACWR had a small-to-moderate association with injury' and 'high heterogeneity was observed'; 'the association was not significant for time-loss injuries'; 'current evidence does not support its use as a stand-alone causal or predictive model.'

citation.title: Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis
citation.authors: Ding L, Weldon A, Xu J, Malone S, Sampaio J, Zhang Z, Zhou Z, Liu X, Han S, Xu K, Wang Y, Yuan P

claims.claim: Running-specific ACWR evidence is inconsistent in direction. In 435 Dutch runners, higher ACWR was inversely associated with running-related injury (an L-shaped decay), while a 24-month study of 23 competitive runners reported an ACWR-injury association, and a 5,205-runner cohort found a negative dose-response for ACWR and no relationship for the week-to-week ratio. ACWR should not be used as a stand-alone runner injury predictor.
claims.evidence: Nakaoka et al. 2021 (435 runners): 'ACWR had an inversely proportional association ... represented by a smooth L-shaped polynomial decay curve'; Dijkhuis et al. 2020 (23 competitive runners): 'ACWR relates to injury'; Frandsen et al. 2025 (5,205 runners): 'A negative dose-response was observed for ACWR' and 'No relationship was identified for the week-to-week ratio.'

citation.title: The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Running-Related Injuries in Dutch Runners: A Prospective Cohort Study
citation.authors: Nakaoka G, Barboza SD, Verhagen E, van Mechelen W, Hespanhol L

claims.claim: In a 5,205-runner prospective cohort, a single session exceeding the longest run in the previous 30 days by more than 30% was associated with higher overuse injury rates: small spikes (>30% to 100%) HRR ~1.31-1.52, and large spikes (>100%) HRR ~3.48. This supports monitoring session distance relative to the recent longest run, not only weekly ACWR.
claims.evidence: Frandsen et al. 2025: 'Significantly increased rates were observed for small spikes (HRR 1.31, 95% CI 1.11-1.55), moderate spikes (HRR 1.52, 95% CI 1.24-1.86), and large spikes (HRR 3.48, 95% CI 2.31-5.24).' 'A significant increase in the rate of running-related overuse injury was observed when the distance of a single session exceeded the longest run in the previous 30 days by more than 30%.'

citation.title: How much running is too much? A 5205-person cohort study
citation.authors: Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, Hulme A, Parner ET, Møller M, Abrahamson J, Sjørup Simonsen N, Sandell Jacobsen J, Ramskov D, Malisoux L, Bertelsen ML, Nielsen RO

claims.claim: Session-RPE load is calculated as RPE (typically Borg CR-10, 0-10) multiplied by session duration in minutes, giving arbitrary units (AU). For example, RPE 6 x 60 min = 360 AU. The method is practical for app-based logging and is valid for quantifying internal training load.
claims.evidence: Foster 2001 introduced the session-RPE method; Halson 2014 states 'session-RPE load is calculated as RPE multiplied by session duration in minutes' and notes that session-RPE is a valid tool for quantifying training load.

citation.title: A new approach to monitoring exercise training
citation.authors: Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, Gottschall L, Hrovatin LA, Parker S, Doleshal P, Dodge C
citation.venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.claim: Session-RPE correlates strongly with objective load measures: in the original validation, session-RPE correlated with summated heart-rate zones at r ~0.88-0.95; a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes found moderate-to-strong correlations with heart rate (r ~0.62-0.85). It is less precise for short, high-intensity intervals and should be complemented by HR/pace when available.
claims.evidence: Halson 2014: 'session-RPE correlated with summated heart-rate zones at r = 0.88-0.95'; Liu et al. 2023 meta-analysis: 'moderate-to-strong correlations with heart rate (r = 0.62-0.85)' and 'session-RPE is a valid method for quantifying training load.'

citation.title: Session-RPE for quantifying the load of different training sessions in endurance athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
citation.authors: Liu Y, Li C, et al.

claims.claim: Training monotony is the mean daily load over a week divided by the standard deviation of daily load (monotony = mean weekly load / SD weekly load). A high value means the week is monotonous, with little day-to-day variation.
claims.evidence: Nobari et al. 2022 define training monotony as 'the mean daily load divided by the standard deviation of daily load'; the metric derives from Foster's monotony/strain approach.

citation.title: Training monotony and strain in professional soccer players: a systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.claim: Training strain is weekly total load multiplied by training monotony (strain = weekly load x monotony). It combines volume and monotony; high strain indicates a high-load, low-variation week.
claims.evidence: Nobari et al. 2022 define training strain as 'weekly total load multiplied by training monotony'; the metric derives from Foster's monotony/strain approach.

citation.title: Training monotony and strain in professional soccer players: a systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.claim: Fatigue monitoring should combine multiple markers (session-RPE, wellness questionnaires, sleep, HRV, HR recovery, and performance) rather than rely on a single measure, and should be interpreted against each athlete's own baseline. No single marker has strong evidence as a definitive fatigue indicator.
claims.evidence: Halson 2014: 'very few of these markers have strong scientific evidence supporting their use, and there is yet to be a single, definitive marker described in the literature'; 'the importance of individualization of load monitoring cannot be over emphasized.'

citation.title: Monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes

claims.claim: HRV-guided training uses daily or weekly HRV (e.g., lnRMSSD) against a rolling baseline to adjust load. Controlled studies support a physiological rationale and some performance benefit, but protocols are heterogeneous and standardized decision rules are lacking; HRV should be one input in a multi-marker framework, not a stand-alone controller.
claims.evidence: Schaffarczyk & Sperlich 2026 SWOT review: strengths include 'a well-established physiological rationale' and 'controlled studies'; weaknesses include 'limited specificity' and 'lack of standardized decision rules'; the main limitation is 'no longer ... the technology but the decision framework.'

claims.claim: RPE can be used to autoregulate session intensity in real time: prescribe a target RPE range (e.g., CR-10 4-6 for moderate, 7-8 for hard) and adjust pace/load to keep RPE in range. In a controlled study, RPE-guided training produced similar physiological adaptations to fixed-intensity training while reducing perceived exertion, supporting RPE as a practical autoregulatory target.
claims.evidence: Bok et al. 2026: 'RPE-guided training produced similar physiological adaptations to fixed-intensity training while reducing perceived exertion.' The authors concluded that RPE-guided training can be used to prescribe and adjust session intensity.

citation.title: RPE-guided training: a randomized controlled trial comparing RPE-guided and fixed-intensity training in recreational runners
citation.authors: Bok D, Rietjens G, Plasqui G, et al.

claims.topic: Real-time autoregulation: HR and wellness signals
claims.claim: Heart rate and wellness/feel can support real-time adjustment, but each has limits: HR lags behind rapid changes in intensity and varies with hydration, heat, and caffeine, while wellness ratings are subjective and should be compared with an individual rolling baseline. Use HR and feel as cross-checks on RPE/pace, not as sole controllers.
claims.evidence: Halson 2014 notes that HR is a valid load marker but has limitations and that subjective questionnaires/diaries are widely used; it recommends combining measures and individualizing interpretation. The review also notes that no single marker is definitive.

citation.title: Monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes

claims.topic: Practical decision rules for the app
claims.claim: A practical app rule set: (1) compute sRPE load = RPE x minutes; (2) compute acute load as a 7-day rolling sum and chronic load as a 28-day rolling average (or EWMA); (3) compute ACWR = acute/chronic and use it only as a contextual flag; (4) compute monotony = mean daily load / SD daily load and strain = weekly load x monotony; (5) avoid single-session distance spikes >30% above the longest run in the prior 30 days; (6) reduce load when wellness/HRV/RPE indicate poor readiness. ACWR should be one input, not a hard threshold.
claims.evidence: Synthesizes formulas from Foster 2001, Halson 2014, and Nobari 2022 with the running-specific cohort findings of Frandsen 2025; Impellizzeri et al. 2020 recommend against fixed ACWR thresholds and urge reliance on progressive overload and athlete response.

citation.title: Training Load and Its Role in Injury Prevention, Part 2: Conceptual and Methodologic Pitfalls
citation.authors: Impellizzeri FM, McCall A, Ward P, Bornn L, Coutts AJ

summary_tier_a: ACWR is a widely used but contested load-management metric: it is defined as acute load divided by chronic load (commonly 1-week over 4-week average), and Gabbett's model proposes a 'sweet spot' around 0.8-1.3, but methodological critiques (mathematical coupling, arbitrary windows, discretization, schedule confounding) and a 2026 meta-analysis show only small-to-moderate, heterogeneous associations and no support for stand-alone causal or predictive use. Running-specific evidence is inconsistent in direction; a large 5,205-runner cohort found that single-session distance spikes >30% above the recent longest run predicted overuse injury, while ACWR showed a negative dose-response. Practical app formulas include sRPE load = RPE x minutes, acute/chronic rolling loads and ACWR, monotony = mean daily load / SD daily load, and strain = weekly load x monotony; use these with wellness, HRV, HR, and RPE as multi-marker contextual signals, not hard thresholds.
unverified: The '10% weekly mileage rule' is a coaching heuristic; no peer-reviewed study validates 10% as a universal safe progression threshold. Running-specific cohort data suggest keeping weekly increases below ~20-30% and avoiding single-session spikes >30% above the recent longest run, but the exact 10% figure is unverified.

Specific ACWR cut-offs (e.g., <0.8, 0.8-1.3, >1.5) and the 'sweet spot' are not validated precision thresholds; the 0.8-1.3 range is a proposed heuristic and has been criticized for methodological flaws.
Training monotony/strain thresholds (e.g., monotony >2.0) are not validated; they should be treated as trend indicators only.
HRV readiness thresholds (e.g., lnRMSSD within 0.5 SD of baseline) are not standardized; no single validated cut-off exists.
notes: Retrieval: PubMed article pages returned a cookie wall, so Europe PMC REST API was used for metadata/abstracts; all citations were checked against Europe PMC records and DOIs/URLs. Scope note: most ACWR evidence is from team sports; running-specific evidence is sparse and inconsistent. The app should treat ACWR, monotony, and strain as contextual load-management signals, not diagnostic thresholds. Schema's citation.type enum lacks 'observational'/'cohort'; prospective cohort studies are labeled 'rct' and their design is stated in the evidence field. sRPE is valid but not perfect; combine with HR/pace and athlete-reported feel. No claims were fabricated; where evidence is thin or observational, confidence is marked medium/low.
